opening: Russia and Ukraine traded heavy long-range strikes on the eve of talks in Abu Dhabi. A gunman killed six people in Kraków, Gadi Eisenkot began trying to form Israel’s government, Qatar took Iran mediation to the White House, and the COP31 climate summit opened in Türkiye.

stories.title: On the eve of US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia sends 317 drones at Ukraine and Ukrainian drones set a refinery near St Petersburg on fire
stories.body: Russia launched 317 drones at Ukraine overnight, 105 of them jet-powered, Ukraine’s air force said, and Russia’s defence ministry said it hit electrical substations in four regions, including around Kyiv. Ukrainian drones started a fire at the KINEF refinery near St Petersburg, more than 1,200 kilometres from the border. The strikes came a day before two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on security guarantees. Moscow is sending a more senior team led by Vladimir Medinsky; Rustem Umerov leads Ukraine’s. France says European officials will attend, which Moscow disputes.
stories.whatChanged: Russia named a more senior delegation, France said Europeans would be in Abu Dhabi despite Moscow’s objections, and both sides stepped up long-range strikes a day before the talks.
stories.whyMatters: These are the first three-way talks since February, and higher-ranking teams and an agenda on security guarantees suggest a more serious round, while attacks on power grids and refineries will shape how both countries get through the winter.
stories.uncertainty: Moscow says European officials will not take part while France says they will; President Trump’s claim that the two sides are very close has not been echoed by either government; damage from the overnight strikes was still being assessed.
stories.watchNext: The opening of talks on Tuesday, November 10, whether European officials are in the room, and a possible meeting of Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.
keyFacts: Russia launched 317 drones overnight into November 9, 105 of them jet-powered, per Ukraine’s air force
Ukraine’s air force said it downed 276 drones and five missiles, with hits recorded at 31 locations
Russian attacks injured 28 people across Ukraine over the past day, the Kyiv Independent reported
The Abu Dhabi talks run over two days from Tuesday, November 10
Russia’s team is led by Vladimir Medinsky and includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin

report.heading: The overnight strikes
paragraphs: Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 317 drones of various types overnight into Monday, 105 of them jet-powered, along with missiles, and that air defences brought down 276 drones and five missiles. Hits were recorded at 31 locations, the Kyiv Independent reported. Russia’s defence ministry said it struck four electrical substations in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, describing the campaign in terms that the Associated Press said amounted to denying Ukrainians heat, light and water before winter. Over the past day Russian attacks injured 28 people across six regions, with the most in Kharkiv.

Ukrainian long-range drones set fire to the KINEF refinery, one of Russia’s largest, near St Petersburg, the Leningrad region’s governor, Alexander Drozdenko, confirmed. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the European Union had agreed to trigger an emergency mechanism to speed up money for repairing Ukraine’s power grid.

report.heading: Who is going to Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: The talks, mediated by the United States, are due to run over two days from Tuesday and will cover security guarantees. The last three-way round, in Geneva in February, made no significant progress. Ukrainska Pravda, citing Bloomberg and the Kremlin, reported that Russia’s delegation will be led by Putin’s aide Vladimir Medinsky and include the deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin and the military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov. Ukraine’s team is led by Rustem Umerov and includes Kyrylo Budanov.

report.heading: Europe’s place and Trump’s claims
paragraphs: France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, told RTL radio on Sunday that Europeans would be represented and that France would take part, AFP reported, while Moscow has said European officials will not join. In a television interview aired on Sunday, Trump said Moscow and Kyiv were very close to a deal and that Ukraine would have a slightly different shape afterwards, without explaining. He also said he would likely meet Putin and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in China later this month.

stories.title: A gunman with far-right views kills six people in Kraków’s Main Square after police say he killed his parents and sister
stories.body: A 24-year-old Polish man opened fire in the Main Square of Kraków’s old town on Saturday afternoon, killing six people, four of them Polish, one British and one from another foreign country, and wounding about 15. Police shot and wounded him, and he died in hospital early on Monday, police said. The bodies of his mother, father and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Prosecutors are treating the attack as a terrorist offence, and Poland held two days of national mourning.
stories.whatChanged: The suspect died in hospital on Monday, prosecutors said they were preparing murder charges that could cover all nine deaths, and officials described him as holding very radical, ultranationalist views.
stories.whyMatters: Mass shootings are rare in Poland, and an attack in one of Europe’s busiest tourist squares by a man officials describe as far-right will test how the country and its neighbours handle legal gun ownership and political extremism.
stories.uncertainty: The suspect has not been officially named and his motive has not been set out in detail; investigators had not formally confirmed that he killed his family; the nationality of one foreign victim was not given.
stories.watchNext: The prosecutors’ account of the investigation now that the suspect has died, the condition of the wounded police officer in a coma, and any proposals to tighten rules on legally held guns.
keyFacts: Six people were killed and about 15 wounded in Kraków’s Main Square on Saturday, November 7
The 24-year-old suspect died in hospital early on Monday, November 9, police said
His parents and sister were found dead at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski
Eleven weapons were recovered; his father legally owned more than ten guns, officials said
Poland held national mourning on November 8 and 9

report.heading: What happened
paragraphs: The gunman opened fire on Saturday afternoon in the Main Square, the centre of Kraków’s old town and one of the most visited places in Poland. Six people were killed: four women and two men. Four were Polish, one was a man from the United Kingdom and one was a woman from another country that officials did not name, the Associated Press reported. About 15 people were wounded. Two police officers who stopped the attacker were taken to hospital; one remained in a coma, according to the region’s governor, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, who praised their intervention.
Police shot and wounded the suspect. Polish police said on Monday that he had died in hospital early that morning, ABC News reported.

report.heading: The suspect and the investigation
paragraphs: Investigators found the bodies of the suspect’s mother, father and sister at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometres north-east of Kraków; they had probably been shot. The interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said the man held very radical, ultranationalist views and was fascinated by far-right ideologies. His father legally owned more than ten guns and he also owned guns, the governor said; 11 weapons were recovered from the home, his car and his person.

Prosecutors opened a case covering murder and attempted murder, including of police officers, and said the acts amounted to a terrorist offence. A prosecutor told ABC News that six murder charges were being prepared, which could rise to nine if investigators confirmed he killed his family.

report.heading: Mourning
paragraphs: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday. The hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s Basilica, which overlooks the square, was paused overnight, the first time it had been missed since the Second World War, and flags were lowered at the European Commission in Brussels.

stories.title: Gadi Eisenkot formally takes on the task of forming Israel’s government and invites Netanyahu’s Likud to join him
stories.body: President Isaac Herzog formally handed Gadi Eisenkot the mandate on Sunday, giving him 28 days to try to form a government. Parties with 67 of the 120 seats recommended him, but that count includes Arab-led parties that several of his potential partners refuse to sit with. Eisenkot called for a national emergency government and invited Likud and the Religious Zionist party to join under his leadership. Benjamin Netanyahu, in a video, urged a unity government of what he called the national camp instead.
stories.whatChanged: The mandate became formal, and both men are now competing to build a unity government, each on his own terms and each looking to the ultra-Orthodox parties.
stories.whyMatters: Whether Israel gets a new prime minister for the first time since 2022 will shape its approach to the war with Iran, Gaza and relations with Washington, and the arithmetic leaves no easy path to 61 seats.
stories.uncertainty: Reports differ on whether Eisenkot would rely on outside support from Arab-led parties for a minority government; the ultra-Orthodox parties have not committed; reports describe the deadline as 28 days, with longer totals cited if extensions are granted.
stories.watchNext: Talks between Eisenkot and United Torah Judaism and Shas, whether Avigdor Liberman’s refusal to depend on Arab parties holds, and any move by Likud lawmakers toward a unity deal.
keyFacts: Herzog formally tasked Eisenkot on Sunday, November 8
Parties with 67 seats recommended Eisenkot and parties with 46 recommended Netanyahu
Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, AFP reported
A Knesset majority is 61 of 120 seats
Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff and would be Israel’s first Sephardic prime minister

report.heading: The mandate
paragraphs: At a ceremony at the president’s office on Sunday, Eisenkot accepted the task of forming a government and said Israel needed a national emergency government, describing the country as approaching a point of no return. Parties holding 67 seats recommended him and parties holding 46 recommended Netanyahu, AFP reported, but the 67 includes Arab-led parties, which won a record number of seats and which several parties in his camp will not govern with.

Eisenkot invited Likud and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist party to join a unity government under his leadership, saying his door was open; Al Jazeera reported that he left open a role for Netanyahu himself. AFP reported that he appears open to starting with a minority government relying on outside votes, while Al Jazeera reported him ruling out work with Arab-led parties.

report.heading: Netanyahu’s answer
paragraphs: In a recorded video on Saturday evening, Netanyahu called for a national unity government made up of the parties of what he calls the national camp, and argued that a government depending on Arab parties would not fight Hamas, Ynet reported. Eisenkot’s Yashar party accused him of hypocrisy and invited Likud members to join a government led by Eisenkot without what it called extremists, the Times of Israel reported.

report.heading: The kingmakers
paragraphs: United Torah Judaism recommended no candidate and its officials told Ynet they expected Shas to follow if they reached agreement with Eisenkot; Shas has so far stayed with Netanyahu. Avigdor Liberman says he will not back a government that depends on Arab parties but has become open to the ultra-Orthodox parties, AFP reported, despite his long campaign for universal military service.

stories.title: Qatar’s prime minister heads to the White House on Iran, as a drone strike on a gas field cuts most of Iraqi Kurdistan’s electricity
stories.body: President Trump is due to meet Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, on Monday to discuss a ceasefire with Iran and a return to nuclear talks. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that Iran’s conditions were unacceptable and no breakthrough was close, while Iran’s foreign minister said its own proposal stood. Late on Sunday a drone struck the Khor Mor gas field in northern Iraq, halting production and cutting the Kurdistan region’s power supply by roughly three-quarters. Nobody has claimed the attack.
stories.whatChanged: Mediation moved to the White House while both sides hardened their public positions, and the war’s attacks on energy sites reached Iraq’s main Kurdish gas field.
stories.whyMatters: Qatar is the main channel between Washington and Tehran, and continued attacks on gas fields, tankers and oil sites keep energy supplies and prices at risk across the Gulf and beyond.
stories.uncertainty: Responsibility for the Khor Mor strike is unknown; Iran’s claims of tankers hitting mines near Hormuz have not been independently confirmed; the outcome of Monday’s meeting is not known.
stories.watchNext: What comes out of the White House meeting, Iran’s formal response to the Qatari plan, Iraq’s investigation into the Khor Mor attack, and further incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.
keyFacts: Trump meets Qatar’s prime minister at the White House on Monday, November 9
A drone hit the Khor Mor gas field’s liquefied gas unit at about 11 PM local time on November 8
Kurdistan’s grid fell from more than 3,700 megawatts to about 1,000, according to reports
A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on November 7, the UK maritime agency said
Brent crude fell toward 97 dollars a barrel on Monday after its biggest weekly drop since 2020

report.heading: Diplomacy moves to Washington
paragraphs: The White House schedule showed Trump meeting Qatar’s prime minister on Monday, with a new ceasefire and a resumption of nuclear talks on the agenda, ANI reported. Before leaving for a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris, Rubio said there had been little progress and called some of Iran’s conditions unacceptable, according to ABC News. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran’s own proposal still stood and required an end to the war on all fronts. Trump told CNN that new strikes were highly unlikely if talks progressed.

report.heading: The Khor Mor attack
paragraphs: A drone struck the liquefied petroleum gas unit at the Khor Mor field in Sulaimani province late on Sunday, starting a large fire that was later put out, Al Jazeera reported. The operator, Dana Gas, said no staff were hurt and production remained suspended, according to Kurdistan24. Because the field feeds the region’s power stations, supply in the Kurdistan region fell from more than 3,700 megawatts to around 1,000, cutting electricity to Erbil, Sulaimani and Duhok. Iraq’s prime minister ordered a joint investigation; no group has claimed the attack.

report.heading: At sea and in the markets
paragraphs: The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said an outbound tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, with the crew safe, Iran International reported. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that tankers using what they called unauthorised routes had struck mines; those claims have not been confirmed. Brent crude slipped toward 97 dollars a barrel on Monday, Nairametrics reported, after falling more than 16 percent last week on hopes for diplomacy.

stories.title: The COP31 climate summit opens in Türkiye late and split over money, with no officials sent by the Trump administration
stories.body: The UN climate conference opened in Antalya on Monday an hour and a half late, after negotiators argued into Sunday night over developing countries’ demands to put climate finance on the agenda. UN Secretary-General António Guterres told delegates the world had entered a new age of climate extremes. Türkiye is inviting countries to a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of energy demand from about a fifth to 35 percent by 2035. Organisers say leaders from 102 countries have confirmed attendance; the Trump administration sent no officials.
stories.whatChanged: Two weeks of talks began with a dispute over finance already delaying the opening, and with a fossil-fuel roadmap left off the formal agenda.
stories.whyMatters: Current national pledges put the world on course for about 2.6 degrees of warming, and poorer countries say the money they need to adapt is a fraction of what they receive.
stories.uncertainty: It was not clear at the opening whether the full agenda had been adopted, and the number of leaders who will actually travel to Antalya has not been confirmed.
stories.watchNext: The leaders’ summit on November 11 and 12, how many countries join the electrification pledge, and how finance for adaptation is handled before the talks close on November 20.
keyFacts: COP31 runs in Antalya from November 9 to November 20, 2026
Organisers say leaders from 102 countries had confirmed as of November 9
The voluntary target is electricity at 35 percent of final energy use by 2035, from about 20 percent
The UN Environment Programme estimates current pledges point to about 2.6 degrees Celsius of warming
Developing countries need about 305 billion dollars a year for adaptation by 2035, the UN estimates; developed countries provided roughly 28 to 32 billion in 2024

report.heading: A late start
paragraphs: The opening ceremony at the Antalya expo centre began 90 minutes behind schedule without explanation, AFP reported, after talks late on Sunday over developing countries’ push to add finance items to the agenda. Greenpeace’s delegation head said developed countries had taken a hard line on a platform agreed last year for discussing how rich countries pay for poorer ones’ climate action. A source told AFP that a climate finance work programme would be included, but that African countries’ call to triple adaptation finance would be discussed under other items rather than separately. A senior EU official warned there was no political will for new funding pledges.

Guterres urged leaders to cut emissions faster, speed a just transition from fossil fuels and deliver finance to vulnerable countries. The COP31 president, Türkiye’s environment minister Murat Kurum, said delay carried one of the heaviest costs in climate action. Australia leads the negotiations under an arrangement that settled a dispute over hosting.

report.heading: What is on the table
paragraphs: The Turkish presidency’s main proposal is a set of voluntary targets: raising electricity to 35 percent of final energy use by 2035, cutting the energy intensity of buildings by at least a quarter, and raising circular use of materials, The Rio Times reported. The EU wants electrification to be clean, which could cause friction over oil, gas and coal. A roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, promised after COP30 ended without explicit language on them, has stalled and is not formally on the agenda.

The UN Environment Programme’s latest reports estimate that fully implemented pledges would lead to about 2.6 degrees of warming this century, and that developing countries need around 305 billion dollars a year for adaptation by 2035.

report.heading: Who is coming
paragraphs: Organisers say heads of state or government from 102 countries had confirmed by Monday, with leaders due on November 11 and 12. Brazil’s President Lula was due to arrive late on Monday. The Trump administration has not sent officials, though a US congressional delegation is attending.

stories.title: Taiwan’s stock market jumps nearly 5 percent after new limits on short selling, while Seoul slips again
stories.whatChanged: The first trading day after Taiwan’s rescue measures brought a sharp rebound in Taipei and Tokyo, but foreign investors kept selling in South Korea.
stories.body: Taiwan’s main index closed up 4.98 percent at 41,680 after regulators cut the share of trading that can be borrowed-share short sales and raised margin requirements, and a state stabilisation fund was cleared to buy. Japan’s Nikkei rose about 2.4 percent after its worst week since 2020. South Korea’s KOSPI ended 0.75 percent lower at 5,022 as foreign investors sold about 865 billion won of shares. The rout last week was driven by fears that the AI building boom will slow.

stories.title: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty, with about 400,000 special votes to count before results on November 27
stories.whatChanged: Seat projections show Christopher Luxon’s coalition one seat over a majority, but special votes, which have tended to favour the left, could still change that.
stories.body: On preliminary results National has 42 seats and Labour 36, and the governing coalition with ACT and New Zealand First holds 67, one more than needed in a 131-seat parliament. About 400,000 special votes remain, with the official result due on November 27. The Opportunity party, with about 6 percent, says it will talk first to National, and former prime minister Helen Clark called the result possibly flawed because of the overhang seats it relies on.

stories.title: A drug that sharply lowered inflammation did not prevent heart attacks, strokes or deaths in a major trial
stories.hook: A clear negative result: hitting the biological target was not enough for patients this sick, though inflammation remains a plausible target earlier in disease.
stories.body: In the ZEUS trial of 6,376 people with heart disease, chronic kidney disease and high inflammation, monthly injections of Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab cut the inflammatory markers hs-CRP by 64 percent and IL-6 by 76 percent. Yet heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths were almost identical: 561 events on the drug against 565 on placebo. Serious infections were slightly more common on the drug. The results were presented at the American Heart Association’s meeting in Chicago and published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
stories.whatChanged: Full peer-reviewed results confirmed that the IL-6 blocker gave no protection, despite doing what it was designed to do to inflammation.
stories.whyMatters: Inflammation has been a leading new target in heart disease, and this was the largest test of blocking IL-6; its failure narrows where the approach may work.
stories.uncertainty: Participants had advanced disease and kidney damage, with about twice the death rate of similar trials, so the result may not apply to healthier patients; the trial was funded by the drug’s maker.
stories.watchNext: Planned trials of IL-6 blockade in earlier-stage disease and of drugs acting further upstream on the NLRP3 inflammasome.
keyFacts: 6,376 participants at 757 sites in 38 countries, followed for a median of about 29 months
561 major cardiovascular events on ziltivekimab versus 565 on placebo
hs-CRP fell 64 percent and IL-6 fell 76 percent on the drug
Serious infections: 20 percent on the drug versus 18 percent on placebo
Published in the New England Journal of Medicine on November 7, 2026

report.heading: The trial
paragraphs: ZEUS was a phase 3, double-blind trial comparing monthly 15-milligram injections of ziltivekimab, an antibody that blocks interleukin-6, with placebo on top of usual care. It enrolled 6,376 adults with atherosclerotic heart disease, significant chronic kidney disease and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of at least 2 milligrams per litre, from 2021 to 2024. Their average age was 69, almost all already took cholesterol-lowering drugs, two-thirds had type 2 diabetes and 42 percent had heart failure.

report.heading: What it found
paragraphs: The main outcome, a combination of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death, occurred 561 times in the ziltivekimab group and 565 times on placebo, a difference that was not significant. Deaths from any cause were 538 and 542. The drug did its biological job, lowering hs-CRP by 64 percent and IL-6 by 76 percent, but that did not translate into fewer events. Overall side effects were similar, though serious infections were somewhat more frequent on the drug, at 20 percent against 18 percent.
More than 6 percent of participants died during the trial, roughly double the rate in comparable studies of patients without severe kidney disease, according to the American Heart Association.

report.heading: What researchers make of it
paragraphs: The lead author, Paul Ridker of Harvard Medical School and Mass General Brigham, cautioned against over-reading the result and called it too little, too late for such a sick population. He pointed out that other anti-inflammatory drugs, canakinumab and low-dose colchicine, have reduced heart attacks and strokes in earlier trials. STAT reported that cardiologists still intend to pursue anti-inflammatory treatments. Next steps include testing IL-6 blockade earlier in the course of disease. The study was funded by Novo Nordisk.

stories.title: The US Justice Department sets up a task force to coordinate AI prosecutions and lawsuits, and to challenge state AI laws
stories.hook: An organisational change rather than new law, but it puts one office in charge of both prosecuting AI misuse and fighting state rules on AI.
stories.body: The Justice Department has created what it calls the Super Intelligence Task Force, under an October 13 memo from Attorney General Todd Blanche. Co-chaired by two senior deputies, it will coordinate criminal and civil cases involving AI misuse by foreign states, criminal groups and companies, recommend enforcement priorities and write prosecution guidance. It absorbs the department’s AI Litigation Task Force, set up in January to challenge state AI laws. The name follows a September executive order telling agencies to say super intelligence instead of artificial intelligence.
stories.whatChanged: AI enforcement at the Justice Department, including its campaign against state AI laws, now runs through one dedicated body.
stories.whyMatters: How federal prosecutors treat AI-enabled fraud and foreign misuse, and how hard Washington pushes against state regulation, will shape the legal ground for AI companies and users.
stories.uncertainty: The department has not described the task force’s staff, budget or timetable for guidance, nor which state laws it will target; it creates no new crimes.
stories.watchNext: The first prosecution guidance, any new lawsuits against state AI laws, and how the task force works with the White House’s Super Intelligence Force led by the intelligence director, Jay Clayton.
keyFacts: Announced on Thursday, November 5, 2026, under an October 13 memo from Attorney General Todd Blanche
Co-chaired by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss
Absorbs the AI Litigation Task Force created in January 2026
Serves as the department’s point of contact with the White House Super Intelligence Force

report.heading: What the department announced
paragraphs: The new body, known as DOJ-SITF, was set up by a memo from Blanche dated October 13 and announced on November 5, Government Executive reported. Blanche wrote that it would ensure American leadership in what the administration now calls super intelligence is not compromised by its misuse. Its jobs are to organise the department’s criminal and civil enforcement involving AI, recommend priorities, draft guidance for prosecuting unlawful AI-related conduct, and coordinate the department’s own lawsuits on AI.
It takes over the work of the AI Litigation Task Force, created in January under Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, to challenge state AI laws seen as conflicting with federal policy.

report.heading: Two different jobs
paragraphs: Analysts at The Neuron noted that the task force combines policing misuse, such as fraud and foreign operations, with an agenda to promote American dominance in AI, including by contesting state regulation. They reported that prosecutors may have to notify the task force before opening AI-related cases, with exceptions for emergencies. The task force is also the department’s link to the White House Super Intelligence Force, which coordinates government dealings with AI companies.

report.heading: The name
paragraphs: The wording follows an executive order in late September directing agencies to use super intelligence in place of artificial intelligence. Government Executive pointed out that the term already has a separate, established meaning: systems that far exceed human intelligence, which is not what the department is describing.

stories.title: Winter rain floods tens of thousands of tents in Gaza, and a collapsing sand bank kills five people, four of them children
stories.body: Heavy rain on Sunday caused a sand mound to collapse onto tents in Deir el-Balah, in central Gaza, killing five people including four children, Al Jazeera reported. Gaza’s government media office said about 70,000 tents were flooded and nearly 400,000 displaced people live in flood-prone areas. Save the Children said shelter supplies were held up at the crossings because Israel was not letting them in. Separately, an Israeli drone strike west of Khan Younis killed two people on Sunday evening, according to the Palestinian news agency WAFA.
stories.whatChanged: The first heavy winter storm turned the shortage of shelter into deaths, more than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire.
stories.whyMatters: Most of Gaza’s population is still living in tents and damaged buildings, so each winter storm brings new risks while aid for shelter remains restricted.
stories.uncertainty: Flood figures come from Gaza’s Hamas-run authorities and could not be independently verified; Israel had not commented on the claim that shelter aid was being held back.
stories.watchNext: Further storms forecast this winter, whether tents and shelter materials are allowed in at the crossings, and continuing deaths from strikes despite the ceasefire.

Al Jazeera reports more than 1,600 people killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire

report.heading: The storm
paragraphs: Heavy rain on Sunday brought a mound of sand down onto tents sheltering displaced families in Deir el-Balah, killing five people, four of them children, Al Jazeera and The New Arab reported. Across the territory, water flooded camps of makeshift shelters. Gaza’s government media office estimated that about 70,000 tents were flooded and that nearly 400,000 displaced people live in areas at risk of flooding. The water left tens of thousands of people without dry shelter across the territory, Al Jazeera reported.

report.heading: Shelter held back
paragraphs: Save the Children said supplies to protect families from the weather were stuck at the border because Israel was blocking their entry, Al Jazeera reported. Israel has not publicly responded to that claim. Aid groups have warned for months that most families in Gaza face the winter in tents or damaged buildings.

report.heading: Strikes continue
paragraphs: On Sunday evening an Israeli drone strike near the Taiba Towers, west of Khan Younis, killed two people, including a woman, according to WAFA, which said several other people were wounded in the same attack. Al Jazeera, citing Gaza’s health authorities, puts the death toll since the October 2025 ceasefire above 1,600, and the total since the war began in 2023 above 74,600. These figures come from authorities in Gaza and could not be independently verified.

watch.text: US-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, November 10, and run for two days.

watch.title: Senate counts
watch.text: Tuesday, November 10, is the last day for mail ballots to arrive in Mississippi’s Senate race, and Alaska releases new batches of ballots on Monday and Tuesday.

watch.title: Leaders at COP31
watch.text: World leaders address the COP31 climate summit in Antalya on Wednesday and Thursday, November 11 and 12.

north-america.summary: Congress returned for its final weeks before the new majority takes over, with a push to impeach Pete Hegseth and a December funding deadline, as Stephen Miller became White House chief of staff. The Justice Department set up an AI task force.

briefs.title: Alaska’s Senate count resumes with Mary Peltola narrowly ahead
briefs.text: The Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 votes, 48.2 percent to 47.9 percent, with about three-quarters counted, the latest Associated Press figures show. New batches of ballots were due on Monday and Tuesday, and ranked-choice tabulation begins on November 18 if no one passes 50 percent.

briefs.title: Canada’s budget adds 11.2 billion dollars for defence but does not price the NATO target
briefs.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s 2026 budget includes 142 billion Canadian dollars in new spending, CTV News reported. The Hub found that it adds 11.2 billion for defence but leaves the cost of reaching NATO’s 2035 spending target unstated.

latin-america.summary: Paraguayan prosecutors searched the detained former president’s house, and Pope Leo XIV began a visit to Argentina. Mexico arrested an alleged cartel commander and Brazil’s president promised fiscal discipline.

briefs.title: Mexico arrests an alleged commander of the Jalisco cartel
briefs.text: Mexican forces arrested Rafael Álvarez, alleged head of a Jalisco New Generation cartel cell, in Zapopan on Sunday, using US intelligence, Al Jazeera reported. He was wounded in a shootout and 19 other people were detained. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch linked him to at least 19 killings, and he faces a US extradition request.

sources.title: Mexico arrests alleged major leader of Jalisco cartel

briefs.title: Lula promises to keep Brazil’s fiscal rules in a national broadcast
briefs.text: In a broadcast on Sunday night, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pledged fiscal responsibility and adherence to the spending rules, Agência Brasil reported. He also said he would propose a public security ministry and free weekend public transport. Brazil’s electoral court is examining a complaint against his re-election ticket.

sources.title: Lula se compromete com responsabilidade fiscal e busca conciliação

briefs.title: Cuba’s president rejects new US sanctions
briefs.text: Miguel Díaz-Canel said Cuba would not be made to yield after Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on eight entities, two people and five ships, including Chinese firms accused of supplying the Cuban military.

sources.title: Cuban Leader Díaz-Canel Defies Rubio's Sanctions: 'We Will Not Be Defeated!'

europe.summary: Poland mourned six people killed in a shooting in Kraków, Russia and Ukraine traded long-range strikes before talks in Abu Dhabi, and the COP31 climate summit opened in Türkiye.

briefs.title: G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Ukraine and Iran
briefs.text: Foreign ministers from the Group of Seven meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday after the venue was moved from Marseille, with Ukraine, the Middle East, Hormuz and energy security on the agenda, France’s foreign ministry said. Marco Rubio said there had been progress on Ukraine’s post-war security arrangements but no breakthrough on Iran, the Associated Press reported. France has signalled there will be no joint communiqué.

briefs.title: Donors meet in Paris to fund repairs to Chernobyl’s protective dome
briefs.text: France’s finance ministry hosts a donor conference on Monday for the shelter over the damaged Chernobyl reactor, AFP reported. About 500 million euros is needed and just over half has been raised.

africa.summary: South Africa’s ANC began weighing coalition talks after its worst local result, and at least 21 people died when a migrant boat sank off Senegal. Ebola keeps spreading in eastern Congo.

briefs.title: At least 21 people die as a boat capsizes off Senegal
briefs.text: A wooden boat capsized on Saturday off the coast of Kébémer department in northern Senegal, killing at least 21 people, with one survivor rescued, Al Jazeera reported. The toll was provisional and the search was continuing.

sources.title: At least 21 dead as small boat sinks off Senegal

briefs.title: Armed attack in Ebola-hit North Kivu kills at least 33
briefs.text: Fighters of the ADF armed group killed at least 33 people in Cantine, about 50 kilometres west of Beni, burning more than 50 houses and a health post, Al Jazeera reported. About 180 patients fled, including suspected Ebola cases and one confirmed case. WHO’s latest count, to November 3, is 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths in Congo.

middle-east.summary: Gadi Eisenkot began trying to form Israel’s government, Qatar took its Iran mediation to the White House, a drone cut most of Iraqi Kurdistan’s power, and winter floods killed five people in Gaza.

briefs.title: Syria prepares to send special forces to Saudi Arabia
briefs.text: About 600 Syrian special forces fighters are expected to deploy to Saudi Arabia within a week, a Syrian official told the Associated Press, as fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis escalates. Saudi Arabia has agreed to lend Syria more than 400 million dollars for reconstruction. Syria’s state news agency denied that its forces were headed to Yemen.

briefs.title: Israeli shelling and demolitions continue in southern Lebanon
briefs.text: Lebanon’s national news agency reported Israeli artillery fire on several villages in the south on Sunday and demolitions in Bani Hayan, with no casualties reported, Prensa Latina said. Lebanon’s health ministry puts the toll since March 2 at 4,390 dead.

sources.title: Israel bombs towns and demolishes buildings in southern Lebanon

asia.summary: Taiwan’s stock market rebounded sharply after new curbs on short selling, Japan’s also rose, and South Korea’s slipped. Malaysia’s dispute over Najib Razak’s house arrest went to the king.

briefs.title: Malaysia’s attorney general seeks an audience with the king over Najib
briefs.text: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the attorney general would seek an audience with the king to clarify the order moving Najib Razak to house arrest, Malay Mail reported. The palace said the decree was clear and must be respected; the attorney general’s office says it is not defying the king but faces conflicting legal readings of Najib’s sentences.

briefs.title: Indonesia names a fourth suspect in a plot to tap the president’s communications
briefs.text: Indonesian police named a fourth suspect in the alleged scheme to intercept President Prabowo Subianto’s communications, Al Jazeera reported. A former national police chief was among three officers arrested on November 3, in a case that reflects tension between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo.

sources.title: Indonesia names fourth wiretapping suspect as political intrigue deepens

oceania.summary: New Zealand’s election result will not be final until November 27, and Vanuatu’s prime minister survived after a no-confidence motion was withdrawn.

briefs.title: No-confidence motion against Vanuatu’s prime minister is withdrawn
briefs.text: Vanuatu’s opposition withdrew its no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Jotham Napat on Monday before it came to a vote, RNZ Pacific reported. The motion had cited the sharing of ministerial posts and alleged misuse of government investment funds; the government said the opposition had no valid grounds.

briefs.title: Taiwan closes its office in Papua New Guinea and blames China
briefs.text: Taiwan said it would close its representative office in Port Moresby, blaming pressure from Beijing, and halt spot purchases of liquefied natural gas from Papua New Guinea as well as medical and scholarship programmes, Al Jazeera reported.
